{{Short description|Transformation that preserves area measure of regions}}
In [[differential geometry]], an '''equiareal map''', sometimes called an '''authalic map''', is a [[smooth map]] from one [[surface (mathematics)|surface]] to another that preserves the [[area]]s of figures.

==Properties==
If ''M'' and ''N'' are two [[Riemannian manifold|Riemannian]] (or [[Pseudo-Riemannian manifold|pseudo-Riemannian]]) surfaces, then an equiareal map ''f'' from ''M'' to ''N'' can be characterized by any of the following equivalent conditions:
* The [[surface area]] of ''f''(''U'') is equal to the area of ''U'' for every [[open set]] ''U'' on ''M''.
* The [[pullback (differential geometry)|pullback]] of the [[volume element|area element]] ''μ''<sub>''N''</sub> on ''N'' is equal to ''μ''<sub>''M''</sub>, the area element on ''M''.
* At each point ''p'' of ''M'', and [[tangent vector]]s ''v'' and ''w'' to ''M'' at ''p'',

<math display=block>\bigl|df_p(v)\wedge df_p(w)\bigr| = |v\wedge w|\,</math>

where <math display=inline>\wedge</math> denotes the Euclidean [[Exterior algebra|wedge product]] of vectors and ''df'' denotes the [[pushforward (differential)|pushforward]] along ''f''.

==Linear transformations==
[[File:Hyperbolic_rotation.gif|thumb|right|200px|Repeated [[squeeze mapping]] applied to a [[hyperbolic sector]] ]]
Every [[Euclidean isometry]] of the [[Euclidean plane]] is equiareal, but the [[converse (logic)|converse]] is not true. In fact, [[shear mapping]] and [[squeeze mapping]] are [[counterexample]]s to the converse.

Shear mapping takes a rectangle to a parallelogram of the same area. Written in matrix form, a shear mapping along the {{mvar|x}}-axis is 
:<math>\begin{pmatrix}1 & v \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \,\begin{pmatrix}x\\y \end{pmatrix} =   \begin{pmatrix}x+vy\\y \end{pmatrix}.</math>

Squeeze mapping lengthens and contracts the sides of a rectangle in a reciprocal manner so  that the area is preserved. Written in matrix form, with &lambda; > 1 the squeeze reads
:<math>\begin{pmatrix}\lambda & 0 \\ 0 & 1/\lambda  \end{pmatrix}\,\begin{pmatrix}x\\y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\lambda x\\ y/\lambda.\end{pmatrix}</math>

A linear transformation <math>\begin{pmatrix}a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}</math> multiplies  areas by the [[absolute value]] of its [[determinant]] {{math|{{abs|''ad'' – ''bc''}}}}. 

[[Gaussian elimination]] shows that every equiareal linear transformation ([[rotation (mathematics)|rotations]] included) can be obtained by composing at most two shears along the axes, a squeeze and (if the determinant is negative), a [[reflection (mathematics)|reflection]].

==In map projections==
{{main|Equal-area map projection}}

In the context of [[Map#Geographic maps|geographic map]]s, a [[map projection]] is called '''[[Map projection#Equal-area|equal-area]]''', '''equivalent''', '''authalic''', '''equiareal''', or '''area-preserving''', if areas are preserved up to a constant factor; embedding the target map, usually considered a subset of '''R'''<sup>2</sup>, in the obvious way in '''R'''<sup>3</sup>, the requirement above then is weakened to:

:<math>|df_p(v)\times df_p(w)|=\kappa|v\times w|</math>

for some {{nowrap|''κ'' > 0}} not depending on <math>v</math> and <math>w</math>.
For examples of such projections, see [[equal-area map projection]].
